1.pericope_label: I cried unto the Lord with my voice: the complaint poured out and the path known to God

schools.summary: Augustine distinguishes the voice of the body from a man own voice and makes thought itself the cry, and reads the pouring out before God as pouring out where he alone sees.

Calvin prefers the second cave and treats the psalm as a recollection of prayers offered there, and makes the pouring out the reverse both of brooding anxiety and of frantic lamentation, holding that only such prayer could account for the restraint shown; Gill argues that the cave was large enough for the prayer to be spoken aloud and makes the complaint one of the psalmist own unbelief.

Henry dismisses the question of which cave as immaterial, holds that the sufferer dared not speak aloud and that mental prayer is vocal to God, and warns against showing our trouble more to ourselves than to him; Spurgeon holds that in the loneliness of the cave the voice could be used freely, and watches the cry grow into an ordered supplication.

Clarke reviews the two caves and prefers the second if the inscription holds, would otherwise refer the psalm to the captivity, and rejects a bishop reading of it as a prayer of the Messiah for want of evidence.

Ellicott renders the overwhelming of the spirit as a muffling that hid the path from the man while God knew it; Keil and Delitzsch identify the caves and describe the unexplored labyrinth of the second.

debates: Which cave does the title mean, and does the title hold? Keil and Delitzsch allow either of two and describe the labyrinth of the second; Clarke prefers the second if the inscription can be depended on and would otherwise refer the psalm to the captives in Babylon; Calvin prefers the second and adds that the psalm must be a later recollection of prayers offered there; Henry says the question is not material.

Was the cry uttered aloud? Gill argues that it was, since the cave was large enough to hold six hundred men unseen and to let them speak unheard; Spurgeon agrees, since in that loneliness the voice could be used freely; Henry answers that the fugitive dared not speak audibly lest it betray him, and that mental prayer is vocal to God; Augustine sets the question aside, holding that a man thought is his cry to the Lord.
outliers: Clarke rejects the title a prayer of the Messiah taken and deserted, given the psalm by a bishop, allowing that it may be so but asking where the evidence is except in a conjectural system of interpretation.

Keil and Delitzsch describe the cave of Engedi as opening from a narrow concealed entrance into so labyrinthine a maze of passages and vaults that the torches and lines of explorers have not to the present time reached its extremities.
themes: a cry that needs no audible voice
trouble told to God rather than to oneself
prayer as the restraint upon revenge
a path hidden from the walker and known to God

4.pericope_label: I looked on my right hand: no man cared for my soul, and the prayer to be brought out of prison

schools.summary: Henry supplies the history of the desertion and calls such friends swallow-friends who are gone when winter comes, and makes the refuge and the portion answer to the poor cave and the poor crown.

Gill reports and rejects the imperative rendering of the verbs and the reading that addresses the right hand of God, and denies that the prison means either purgatory or the body, taking it of the cave or of the straits that pressed him.

Clarke keeps the prison to the cave whose mouth the enemy held, quotes an old Psalter that takes it of the corruption of the body, and renders the closing verb as crowning, with the pious joining to make him king; Wesley explains the right hand as the place of a patron and has the righteous flock to him rejoicing.

Ellicott restores the Hebrew imperatives against the ancient versions for the sake of liveliness, prefers the sense that the righteous are waiting rather than compassing, and suggests that the word prison gave rise to the inscription; Keil and Delitzsch note that this is the only place in the Psalter where distress is called a prison and find the poet less alone than he seemed.

debates: Are the verbs of the fourth verse past or imperative? Gill reports that some render them as imperatives addressed either to the psalmist own soul or to God, and that one commentator addressed them to the right hand of God, which he rejects since looking cannot be ascribed to a hand; Ellicott takes the rejected side, holding that the received version follows the ancient versions in turning Hebrew imperatives into historic tenses and that the psalm loses in liveliness by the change.

What do the righteous do at the close? Ellicott notes that the verb is used in a hostile sense elsewhere and follows the old Greek in rendering that the righteous are waiting until God deals bountifully; Clarke renders that they shall crown him and suggests that the pious would join to make him king once the persecutor was dead; Wesley has them flock to him to rejoice; Keil and Delitzsch make them a whole congregation joining in praise, so that the poet is not so alone as he seemed.
outliers: Ellicott turns the word prison against the inscription, holding that since the expression must be figurative of distress it was probably this very word that gave rise to the title about the cave.
Clarke old Psalter takes the prison to be the corruption of the body, which corruption is bodily pain in which the soul is in anguish, and looks for all praise to follow in the house of God.
themes: a look for help that finds none
God taken as refuge and as portion
the righteous gathered at the deliverance
